title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
abstract: We propose a criterion for discrimination against a specified sensitive attribute in supervised learning, where the goal is to predict some target based on available features. Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy. In line with other studies, our notion is oblivious: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individualfeatures. We study the inherent limits of defining and identifying biases based on such oblivious measures, outlining what can and cannot be inferred from different oblivious tests. We illustrate our notion using a case study of FICO credit scores.

claims.text: Equalized odds requires a predictor and protected attribute to be independent conditional on the true outcome variable.
Equal opportunity requires equal true positive rates across protected attribute groups for the advantaged outcome.
Optimal equalized odds derived predictors can be constructed from learned binary predictors using linear programming post-processing.
An optimal equalized odds predictor can be derived directly from the Bayes optimal regressor and the protected attribute.

The expected loss of an equalized odds classifier derived from an approximate regressor is bounded by twice the square root of two times the conditional Kolmogorov distance to the Bayes optimal regressor.
Oblivious fairness tests cannot distinguish between different causal dependency structures that share identical joint distributions over outcome, protected attribute, and score.
On FICO credit data at an 82% non-default profitability threshold, a race-blind threshold gets 99.3% of maximal profit.
On FICO credit data at an 82% non-default profitability threshold, equal opportunity gets 92.8% of maximal profit.
On FICO credit data at an 82% non-default profitability threshold, equalized odds gets 80.2% of maximal profit.
On FICO credit data at an 82% non-default profitability threshold, demographic parity gets 69.8% of maximal profit.

limitations.text: Demographic parity permits accepting qualified applicants in one group and unqualified individuals in another, and severely reduces utility when the target variable is correlated with the protected attribute.
Oblivious tests cannot distinguish between underlying causal dependency structures that have identical joint distributions over target, protected attribute, and score.
Equalized odds forces the classifier performance to be bounded by the pointwise minimum ROC curve among protected groups, requiring all groups to be classified as poorly as the hardest group.
The framework relies on access to reliable labeled target data, which may be difficult to obtain, unobserved, or inherently biased in practice.

methodologies.name: Post-processing non-discrimination derivation
methodologies.description: Minimizes expected classification loss subject to equalized odds or equal opportunity constraints by solving a linear program or conducting ternary search over threshold ROC curves.
conditions: Known joint distribution of score, protected attribute, and target variable
